sentences.text: Scalamagnus is known from a single species, S. tropicensis, represented by one skull and two partial skeletons.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is an almost complete, well-preserved skeleton measuring 3.2 meters in length that includes most of the skull.
The holotype skeleton is associated with 289 gastroliths, a feature unusual for most polycotylids which typically lack such stones.
Most of these stones were small, with about three-quarters weighing less than 2 grams and a mean mass of 1.9 grams.
The fossils were collected between 2003 and 2005 by the Museum of Northern Arizona from a single locality in the Tropic Shale of Utah.
The characteristics of the gastroliths suggest the animal obtained them from rivers along the western side of the Western Interior Seaway.
A 2023 study reclassified the species D. tropicensis into its own new genus, Scalamagnus.
Scalamagnus lived during the early Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 93.5 to 91 million years ago.
The fossil record for Scalamagnus spans from 93.9 to 89.8 million years ago within the Turonian stage.
